opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a genuinely welcome development, and in some ways a long overdue one. For years, people in the biosecurity community have argued that gene synthesis is one of the clearest chokepoints we have. If someone wants to build a dangerous pathogen, at some point they need the physical DNA. Screening those orders, checking both the sequence and the customer, is one of the few places where you can intervene before something goes badly wrong.

What's notable is who is saying it now. When the AI companies call for mandatory screening, they're implicitly acknowledging something important: their models may lower the knowledge barrier to misusing biology. They can try to put guardrails on the models themselves, and they should, but they know those guardrails can be jailbroken, and open-weight models exist regardless. So they're pointing downstream to the physical bottleneck, which I think is quite sensible. It's defence in depth.

That said, I'd add a few caveats.

First, "mandatory" and "around the world" are doing a lot of work in that sentence. Today, much screening is voluntary. Many reputable providers do it, often through industry consortia, but coverage is uneven, and a determined bad actor can shop around for a provider, or a jurisdiction, that doesn't screen. A patchwork doesn't really solve the problem. You need something close to universal coverage, which means international coordination, and that's slow and hard.

Second, the technology is moving. Benchtop synthesizers let labs make DNA in-house, so screening at the provider level doesn't capture everything. Any serious regime has to think about the devices themselves, building screening into the machines and controlling who can buy them and the reagents.

Third, screening itself has to keep pace with AI. Traditional screening relies largely on similarity to known sequences of concern. But if AI tools can help design sequences that are functionally dangerous but don't look like anything on a list, homology-based screening starts to break down. So there's a slight irony: the same capabilities that make screening more urgent also make it harder to do well. We need investment in function-based screening and better shared databases.

And finally, I'd be cautious about letting this become a way of passing the buck. It's good that AI developers support screening, but it shouldn't replace their own responsibility to evaluate and mitigate biological risks in their models. Screening is one layer. It's not the whole answer.

So overall: strongly positive, the right instinct, but the hard work is in implementation, global coverage, and keeping the screening technology ahead of the threat.

r001.rationale: The response discusses screening as a biosecurity intervention and its implementation challenges, but does not identify avoided costs from engineered biological incidents as the main economic benefit.

r002.rationale: The response says AI models may lower misuse barriers and warns developers not to pass the buck, but it does not criticize the companies for asking legislators to address risks they increase by releasing capabilities into the public domain.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think it's a welcome development, and a slightly surprising one. Historically, the biosecurity community has been pushing for synthesis screening for the better part of two decades, and the frontier AI labs have, in a fairly short space of time, become some of the loudest voices calling for it to be mandatory rather than voluntary. That's a good thing. When OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind and others say "we're worried that our models could lower the barrier to acquiring dangerous biological capabilities, and the chokepoint we'd like to see hardened is the point where digital sequence information becomes physical DNA," they're pointing at exactly the right place in the pipeline.

So my first reaction is: yes, good, more of this.

My second reaction is a little more cautious, for a few reasons.

The first is that it's worth being clear-eyed about why the labs are making this call. Part of it is genuine concern, and I don't want to be cynical about that. But part of it is also that screening shifts the locus of responsibility away from the model developer and onto the synthesis provider. If you're an AI company, it's much more comfortable to say "the fix is downstream, at the DNA foundry" than to say "the fix is that we should constrain what our models can do, or slow down what we're deploying." Both can be true. But we shouldn't let the first become a substitute for the second. Screening is a backstop, not a license to be less careful upstream.

The second concern is that mandatory screening is genuinely hard to get right, and the details matter enormously. What exactly are we screening against? A list of known select agents and toxins is a reasonable start, but it's exactly the kind of thing that a capable adversary, with or without AI assistance, might design around. Function-based screening, looking at what a sequence does rather than what it matches, is where we need to go, and that's technically much harder and much more contested. Who maintains the databases? Who has access to them? Because a list of "the most dangerous sequences we know of" is itself a sensitive artefact. And how do you handle the benchtop synthesizers that are increasingly being sold into labs, where there's no central provider in the loop at all? If you mandate screening at the big commercial providers and leave benchtop devices unaddressed, you've just moved the problem.

Third, "around the world" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. Screening regimes are only as strong as their weakest jurisdiction. The US has moved on this, the UK has published guidance, the EU is thinking about it. But if a provider in a jurisdiction with no requirements will happily ship an unscreened order, then the global mandate is really only a mandate for the countries that already took this seriously. That means we need something closer to an international standard, with real harmonisation, and ideally some kind of mutual recognition, so that compliant providers in one country are treated as compliant elsewhere. The International Gene Synthesis Consortium and the IBBIS work on common mechanisms are a good foundation, but they're voluntary, and voluntary is not the same as universal.

And finally, I'd want the AI companies to put something behind the words. If they think this matters, there are concrete things they can do: fund the development of better screening tools, including open ones; share threat information about what their models can and can't do to help calibrate what "dangerous" means in practice; and condition access to their most capable biology-relevant systems on users operating within screened supply chains. That would be a much stronger signal than a joint letter.

So, to sum up: I assess it as directionally right and politically useful, because when the labs say this it gets heard by policymakers who have been ignoring biosecurity folks for years. But I'd grade it as an opening move, not a solution. The hard part is implementation, coverage of the gaps like benchtop synthesis and non-compliant jurisdictions, and making sure the AI developers don't treat it as an outsourcing of their own responsibilities.

r001.rationale: The response discusses screening as a biosecurity backstop but does not identify avoided costs from engineered biological incidents or economic benefit as the main reason to make screening mandatory.

r002.rationale: The response says AI companies should not use downstream screening as a substitute for constraining models or slowing deployment. It does not clearly criticize them for asking legislators to address risks they materially increase by releasing capabilities into the public domain.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a welcome call. If AI companies are concerned that their models could make it easier to design something biologically dangerous, then screening orders for synthetic DNA is a sensible place to intervene. You still need to get from information on a screen to physical material, and that gives us an opportunity to prevent misuse.

But I would distinguish calling for mandatory screening from having an effective screening system. You need to assess both the sequence being ordered and who is ordering it. You also need a way to deal with concerning orders, standards that can adapt as capabilities change, and some assurance that providers actually follow those standards.

The international dimension matters because a requirement in one country can be undermined if someone can simply order from a provider elsewhere. That doesn’t mean we should wait for universal agreement before doing anything. It means national requirements need to be accompanied by work to broaden adoption and make compliance affordable.

So I’m positive about the direction. But synthesis screening is one layer of protection, and supporting it doesn’t remove the responsibility of AI companies to assess and mitigate the risks of their own systems.

r001.rationale: The response calls screening an opportunity to prevent misuse but does not identify avoided costs from engineered biological incidents as the main economic benefit.

r002.rationale: It says AI companies remain responsible for assessing and mitigating their systems’ risks, but does not criticize them for asking legislators to address risks they increased by releasing capabilities publicly.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a welcome call. Screening DNA synthesis orders is one of the practical ways we can reduce the risk that someone uses AI to help create a biological threat. But the important word is mandatory. If responsible providers screen their orders and others don’t, someone can simply go to a provider that doesn’t ask questions.

And it needs to be international, because DNA can be ordered across borders. You need a common baseline for checking who the customer is and whether what they’re ordering raises concerns, with a process for resolving legitimate research orders that get flagged.

I would also distinguish calling for this from making it work. Who sets the standards? Who checks that screening is effective? How do smaller providers afford it? Those implementation questions really matter. So I’m pleased to see AI companies supporting this, but synthesis screening is one layer of protection, and their support needs to translate into concrete action.

r001.rationale: The response discusses screening as a way to reduce biological-threat risk, but does not identify avoided costs from engineered incidents as the main economic benefit.

r002.rationale: The response raises implementation questions but does not criticize AI companies for asking legislators to address risks their public releases materially increase.
